title: Who Are the "Friends of the Court"?
hook: Most briefs a supreme court reads are filed by people who aren't suing anyone. The amicus brief is how outside interests get a say in a case they are not party to.
key_points: An amicus curiae — 'friend of the court' — brief is filed by someone who is not a party to the case but has a stake in how it comes out.
Filers range from trade associations and advocacy groups to states, scholars, and former officials.
The justification is expertise: amici supply context, industry facts, or consequences the two parties have no incentive to raise.
The worry is influence: an amicus can push arguments neither party made, and who paid for the brief is not always visible.
Court rules generally require disclosing whether a party helped write or fund a brief, but not the identity of every backer.
content_html: When a high-profile case reaches a supreme court, the two parties file their briefs — and then a much larger stack arrives from everyone else. These are amicus curiae briefs, literally "friend of the court" filings, submitted by people and organizations that are not suing or being sued but care a great deal about the outcome. SCOTUSblog's Amy Howe takes up the obvious question: who exactly are these friends?
extra_html: The filers are a cross-section of organized political life: trade associations and companies, advocacy groups on every side, state governments, groups of law professors, former judges and officials, sometimes a single expert. The defence of the practice is straightforward. A case is argued by two parties with narrow interests, and a ruling may reshape an entire industry, policy area, or body of law that neither of them represents; amici let the court hear about those consequences before it decides. The criticism is equally straightforward. An amicus is not bound by either party's strategy, so a brief can float a theory neither side wanted to argue, and briefs are sometimes coordinated — a campaign of filings designed to make a position look broadly held. Court rules address part of this by requiring disclosure of whether a party to the case authored or paid for a brief, but they generally do not force an organization to name the donors behind it. That gap is the heart of the ongoing argument over amicus practice: everyone agrees the court benefits from outside expertise; the dispute is over how much the court should know about where that expertise came from. (U.S. practice; most apex courts have some equivalent third-party intervention.)

related.title: How the Supreme Court Decides a Case
related.hook: A top court hears only a sliver of the cases that beg for its attention — and the path from petition to ruling runs through written briefs, a public argument, and a vote taken in secret.

related.title: Interest Groups & Lobbying
related.hook: Between elections, organized groups press their case to government every day. Lobbying is how that pressure is applied — and it's both a feature and a worry of democracy.

related.title: The Judiciary & Judicial Review
related.hook: Courts don't just settle disputes between people — through judicial review, many can also strike down a law or an official act that violates the constitution.

flashcards.prompt: Who files an amicus curiae brief, and why are they allowed to?
flashcards.back_html: Someone who is not a party to the case but has a stake in the outcome. The rationale is expertise — supplying context and consequences the two sides may have no reason to raise.

flashcards.prompt: What is the main transparency concern about amicus briefs?

choices.text: Who funded or organized the brief is not always visible to the court or the public
They are filed in secret and never published
Only the parties to the case may read them

flashcards.explanation_html: Rules typically require disclosing a party's involvement in writing or funding a brief, but not every backer behind an amicus filer.

flashcards.prompt: Why can an amicus brief matter beyond simply repeating a party's position?

choices.text: It can introduce arguments or facts that neither party chose to raise
It counts as an extra vote in the case
It obliges the court to hear oral argument from the filer

flashcards.explanation_html: Amici are not bound by either side's litigation strategy, so they can put new framings and consequences in front of the justices.
